prompt: Write an email to a colleague about the weather spoiling your garden plans. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the email only.
final_message:
Subject: The garden, and the weather's opinion of it

Dear Martin,

I write to report that the weather has taken a firm position against my garden, and has not been shy about it.

You may recall that I had set aside this past weekend for the great autumn clearing. The plan was modest. I would pull the spent bean vines, turn over the south bed, and put in the garlic, which ought to be in the ground before the cold arrives in earnest. I had even sharpened the hoe, an act I perform perhaps once a year and with some ceremony. The forecast, which I consulted only a few times an hour, promised a dry Saturday. It was lying.

The rain began a little before eight and showed no interest in stopping. By noon the south bed was a shallow lake, and the path between the rows had become the sort of mud that takes a boot and keeps it. I stood at the back door with my coffee and watched the water gather in the low corner, where, I am told, I once decided that drainage was a matter for the next owner. I am the next owner. I have been the next owner for eleven years.

Sunday was no better, though it did vary the program with a stiff wind. The wind took down the last of the tomato cages, which I had meant to retire in an orderly fashion, and carried the lid of the compost bin somewhere into the neighbor's yard. I have not yet asked for it back; the situation seems to call for diplomacy, as these things go between states.

The garlic, meanwhile, sits in a paper bag on the kitchen counter, and my wife has begun to look at it the way one looks at a guest who has stayed past the agreed date. I am assured that it will keep a week or two, and that the ground will dry out eventually; it generally does, if one is willing to be patient, which is the one crop I have never grown well.

I mention all this partly because you asked how the garden was getting on, and partly because I suspect you have your own plans in the path of this weather. If you have bulbs to plant, I would not wait for a better weekend. I have waited for several, and they have all declined to appear.

If the ground at your end is any drier than mine, I would be glad to hear of it. I will report again once I can see the south bed without a boat.

Walter
